topics.name: Network Fundamentals
topics.description: Understand what networks are, how hosts communicate, and how to reason about basic network designs.

topics.name: Models & Layers
topics.description: Use the OSI and TCP/IP models to understand encapsulation and locate network responsibilities.

topics.name: Network Devices & Roles
topics.description: Distinguish switches, routers, access points, firewalls, modems, and ONTs by what each one does.

topics.name: Ethernet, MAC & ARP
topics.description: Understand local Ethernet delivery, MAC addresses, switches, ARP resolution, and common frame issues.

topics.name: Network Media & Physical Layer
topics.description: Compare copper Ethernet, fiber, link signals, pair layout, and physical symptoms that affect link reliability.

topics.name: IPv4 Addressing
topics.description: Read IPv4 addresses, prefixes, masks, network IDs, host addresses, and default-gateway relationships.

topics.name: Subnetting & Address Planning
topics.description: Calculate subnet ranges and design address blocks for realistic host and growth requirements.

topics.name: IPv6 Addressing
topics.description: Read IPv6 notation, prefix boundaries, link-local addresses, Neighbor Discovery, and dual-stack concepts.

topics.name: Switching & Routing
topics.description: Learn how Layer 2 switching differs from Layer 3 routing and how routers choose next hops.

topics.name: VLANs & Trunking
topics.description: Segment Layer 2 networks, understand access ports and 802.1Q trunks, and identify inter-VLAN routing requirements.

topics.name: Dynamic Routing & OSPF Basics
topics.description: Understand why routing protocols exchange reachability information and how OSPF builds shortest-path routes.

topics.name: Transport & Ports
topics.description: Compare TCP and UDP and understand ports, sockets, connection behavior, and application transport choices.

topics.name: Network Services: DHCP & DNS
topics.description: Explain how devices obtain IP configuration and how domain names resolve to network addresses.

topics.name: NAT, PAT & Private Networks
topics.description: Understand address translation, private IPv4 ranges, port translation, and the limits of NAT as a security control.

topics.name: Wireless Networking
topics.description: Understand Wi-Fi association, bands, channels, interference, roaming, and practical wireless troubleshooting.

topics.name: Troubleshooting & Network Security Basics
topics.description: Use layered troubleshooting, isolate faults systematically, and apply basic network safeguards.

topics.name: ACLs & Network Access Control
topics.description: Understand permit/deny rules, rule order, least privilege, and safe validation of network filters.

topics.name: Network Diagnostic Tools
topics.description: Use ping, traceroute, ipconfig or ip, nslookup or dig, and socket tools to isolate network problems.

topics.name: Packet Analysis with Wireshark
topics.description: Read packet fields and display filters to investigate DNS, TCP handshakes, retransmissions, and basic protocol behavior.

topics.name: Nmap & Service Discovery
topics.description: Use Nmap responsibly to inventory authorized systems and understand host discovery, port states, and service detection.

topics.name: Network Monitoring & Performance
topics.description: Use baselines, interface counters, availability checks, latency, loss, and logs to understand network health.

topics.name: Integrated Network Labs
topics.description: Combine addressing, switching, routing, services, packet analysis, and troubleshooting into documented scenarios.

topics.name: Operating System Fundamentals
topics.description: Understand the kernel, user and kernel modes, system calls, drivers, and OS responsibilities.

topics.name: Processes & Threads
topics.description: Learn the difference between programs, processes, threads, process states, and context switching.

topics.name: CPU Scheduling
topics.description: Compare FCFS, shortest-job-first, priority, round-robin, response time, waiting time, and time quanta.

topics.name: Concurrency, Synchronization & Deadlocks
topics.description: Understand race conditions, critical sections, locks, semaphores, and the conditions that can produce deadlock.

topics.name: Memory Management & Virtual Memory
topics.description: Understand address spaces, paging, page tables, TLBs, page faults, and memory pressure.

topics.name: File Systems & Permissions
topics.description: Understand files, directories, metadata, permissions, mounts, and the difference between names and storage objects.

topics.name: I/O, Interrupts & Device Drivers
topics.description: Explain polling, interrupts, DMA, device drivers, buffering, and the path between applications and hardware.

topics.name: Boot Process & Linux Overview
topics.description: Follow the path from firmware through bootloader and kernel to userspace and understand Linux distributions.

topics.name: Linux Shell & Command-Line Basics
topics.description: Navigate a shell, understand commands and arguments, use quoting, and compose commands with pipes and redirection.

topics.name: Linux Filesystem Navigation
topics.description: Explore the Linux directory hierarchy, absolute and relative paths, mount points, and important system directories.

topics.name: Linux Users, Groups & Permissions
topics.description: Read Unix permission bits and use ownership, groups, sudo, and least-privilege access safely.

topics.name: Text Processing & CLI Workflows
topics.description: Inspect files and logs with grep, less, head, tail, sort, uniq, and safe shell pipelines.

topics.name: Linux Process & Resource Tools
topics.description: Inspect process IDs, CPU and memory usage, signals, priorities, and active sockets using read-only diagnostic commands.

topics.name: Linux Services & systemd
topics.description: Understand service units, startup targets, service status, logs, and safe service lifecycle troubleshooting.

topics.name: Linux Networking Fundamentals
topics.description: Inspect Linux interfaces, routes, DNS configuration, listening sockets, and host connectivity using standard tools.

topics.name: Linux Storage & Filesystems Operations
topics.description: Inspect disks, partitions, mounted filesystems, free space, inodes, and storage pressure without risking data.

topics.name: Linux Logs & System Troubleshooting
topics.description: Use journalctl and log files to correlate events, interpret timestamps, and diagnose service or boot failures.

topics.name: Bash Scripting & Automation
topics.description: Create safe, repeatable shell scripts using variables, conditions, loops, exit statuses, and quoted arguments.

topics.name: Virtualization & Containers
topics.description: Distinguish virtual machines, hypervisors, containers, images, isolation, and resource boundaries.

topics.name: Linux Security & System Hardening
topics.description: Apply least privilege, updates, SSH hygiene, service exposure review, and secure configuration basics.

questions.prompt: In the OSI model, which layer is primarily responsible for logical addressing and routing packets between networks?
questions.objective: Identify the OSI network layer's core responsibility.
questions.explanation: The network layer handles logical addressing and forwarding across interconnected networks. The data-link layer handles local frame delivery.

choices.text: Physical
Data Link
Network
Transport

questions.prompt: The OSI model is a conceptual reference model; real network protocols do not have to map one-to-one to its seven layers.
questions.objective: Distinguish a reference model from a protocol implementation.
questions.explanation: OSI provides a useful way to discuss functions, but actual protocol suites can combine or divide those functions differently.

choices.text: True
False

questions.prompt: A workstation is sending an IPv4 packet to another device on the same LAN. It knows the destination IP address but has no cached MAC address for it. Which protocol can help it discover the local Ethernet address?
questions.objective: Explain how an IPv4 host resolves a local next-hop Ethernet address.
questions.explanation: ARP maps a protocol address such as IPv4 to a local hardware address used for Ethernet delivery. The host broadcasts an ARP request on the local link.

choices.text: DNS
ARP
DHCP
NTP

questions.prompt: Which statements describe common Ethernet switch behavior? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Describe how a basic Ethernet switch learns and forwards frames.
questions.explanation: A learning switch records source MAC addresses on incoming ports and uses its forwarding table to send known unicast frames toward the relevant port. Each switch port is its own collision domain in switched full-duplex Ethernet.

choices.text: It can learn source MAC addresses and associate them with ingress ports.
It routes packets between different IP networks by default.
Each switched port is a separate collision domain.
It must rewrite every frame's source MAC address.

questions.prompt: For a conventional IPv4 /27 subnet, how many usable host addresses are available after excluding the network and broadcast addresses?
questions.objective: Calculate usable host capacity from an IPv4 prefix length.
questions.explanation: A /27 leaves 5 host bits, for 2^5 = 32 total addresses. In a conventional subnet, the network and broadcast addresses are reserved, leaving 30 host addresses.

questions.prompt: The dotted-decimal IPv4 subnet mask 255.255.255.0 corresponds to prefix length /____.
questions.objective: Convert a common IPv4 subnet mask to CIDR notation.
questions.explanation: The first three octets contain 24 one-bits, so the prefix is /24.

questions.prompt: UDP itself guarantees that datagrams arrive in order and are not duplicated.
questions.objective: Recognize guarantees that UDP does not provide by itself.
questions.explanation: UDP provides a lightweight datagram service and does not guarantee delivery, ordering, or duplicate protection.

choices.text: True
False

questions.prompt: An application needs an ordered, reliable byte stream between endpoints. Which transport protocol is the usual fit?
questions.objective: Choose a transport protocol based on an application's delivery needs.
questions.explanation: TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream. Applications using UDP must tolerate or handle loss and ordering themselves when those properties matter.

choices.text: ARP
TCP
UDP
ICMP

questions.prompt: A DHCP server can provide which configuration details to a client? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Identify typical network settings delivered through DHCP.
questions.explanation: DHCP carries host configuration parameters and can supply items such as an address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS server information.

choices.text: An IP address lease
A default gateway option
DNS resolver information
The user's application passwords

questions.prompt: A DNS A record associates a domain name with which kind of address?
questions.objective: Recognize common DNS record purposes.
questions.explanation: An A record maps a DNS name to an IPv4 address. An AAAA record is used for IPv6 addresses.

choices.text: An IPv4 address
An Ethernet MAC address
A TCP session number
A file-system path

questions.prompt: A packet is destined for an IP network that is not directly connected to the sender's LAN. Which device normally forwards it toward another network?
questions.objective: Differentiate basic switching from IP routing.
questions.explanation: A router selects a next hop using network-layer addressing and its routing information. A basic Layer 2 switch forwards Ethernet frames within a local broadcast domain.

choices.text: Router
Repeater
Patch panel
Wireless access point only

questions.prompt: Several private-addressed home devices share one public IPv4 address for outbound connections. Which technique most likely lets the router keep those simultaneous sessions distinct?
questions.objective: Explain the purpose of port translation in address sharing.
questions.explanation: Port Address Translation (PAT), often grouped under NAT, uses transport-layer port mappings to distinguish multiple internal flows using a shared public address.

choices.text: PAT
ARP poisoning
STP
T568B

questions.prompt: Fiber-optic links carry information using light rather than electrical signals in copper conductors.
questions.objective: Compare the signaling medium used by fiber and copper cabling.
questions.explanation: Fiber guides optical signals through glass or plastic fiber, while copper Ethernet uses electrical signaling over conductors.

choices.text: True
False

questions.prompt: Why are twisted pairs used in balanced copper Ethernet cabling?
questions.objective: Describe how pair twisting helps reduce interference.
questions.explanation: Twisting helps reduce the impact of electromagnetic interference and crosstalk on balanced pairs. It does not make a link immune to all noise or installation faults.

choices.text: To reduce interference and crosstalk
To convert IPv4 into IPv6
To assign MAC addresses
To provide optical power to fiber

questions.prompt: A Windows laptop shows an IPv4 address beginning with 169.254 and cannot reach its configured gateway. What should you check first?
questions.objective: Use a host address symptom to guide a safe first troubleshooting step.
questions.explanation: A 169.254/16 link-local address commonly appears when a Windows host has not obtained a DHCP lease. Check link status, the DHCP server or relay path, and the client's lease state before changing unrelated settings.

choices.text: DHCP connectivity and the local link
The remote web server's TLS certificate
The laptop's DNS cache only
The public route to an unrelated network

questions.prompt: Which are sensible baseline steps for reducing access risk on a small network? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Apply least privilege and secure administration basics.
questions.explanation: Unique credentials, timely updates, and limiting access to only what is needed reduce common risks. No single control guarantees a network is secure.

choices.text: Replace default administrative credentials.
Apply security updates.
Allow every device unrestricted inbound access.
Grant users only the access they need.

questions.prompt: Which part of an operating system typically manages privileged access to hardware and core system resources?
questions.objective: Describe the kernel's central role.
questions.explanation: The kernel is the privileged core that manages resources such as CPU time, memory, and device access. User applications request services through system-call interfaces.

choices.text: Kernel
Text editor
User's home directory
DNS resolver

questions.prompt: User mode normally permits an application to execute every privileged hardware instruction directly.
questions.objective: Explain the purpose of separating user mode from kernel mode.
questions.explanation: The privilege boundary prevents ordinary applications from directly executing privileged operations. They request protected services through controlled interfaces such as system calls.

choices.text: True
False

questions.prompt: Compared with separate processes, threads within one process commonly share which resource?
questions.objective: Distinguish process-level resources from per-thread execution state.
questions.explanation: Threads in a process commonly share its address space and resources, while each thread has its own execution state such as registers and stack.

choices.text: The process address space
A separate private address space for every thread
The same instruction pointer at all times
A guaranteed dedicated CPU core

questions.prompt: A CPU scheduler switches from one runnable process to another and later restores the first process. What saved state lets the first process continue?
questions.objective: Explain what context switching preserves.
questions.explanation: A context switch saves and restores execution state, including register values and the instruction position, so each scheduled process can resume.

choices.text: The process execution context
Only the DNS cache
The Ethernet switch table
The display resolution

questions.prompt: In round-robin CPU scheduling, what happens when a runnable task uses its full time quantum and is not finished?
questions.objective: Describe the basic round-robin scheduling rule.
questions.explanation: The scheduler preempts the task at the end of its time slice and places it back in the ready queue, allowing another runnable task to run.

choices.text: It is moved to the ready queue for a later turn.
It is automatically terminated.
It permanently owns the CPU.
Its memory is immediately erased.

questions.prompt: The finite time slice assigned to a task in round-robin scheduling is commonly called a time ____.
questions.objective: Use standard terminology for a round-robin time slice.
questions.explanation: A time quantum (or time slice) is the maximum interval a task can run before the scheduler considers another task.

questions.prompt: Two threads increment a shared counter. Each performs a read, adds one, and writes back. Some increments disappear under concurrent execution. What is the likely issue?
questions.objective: Recognize a race caused by an unsynchronized read-modify-write sequence.
questions.explanation: The operations can interleave so both threads read the same old value and overwrite one another's update. A suitable synchronization mechanism can make the critical section safe.

choices.text: A race condition
A DNS cache miss
External fragmentation
A bootloader timeout

questions.prompt: Which conditions are part of the classic set of necessary conditions for deadlock? Select all four.
questions.objective: Recall the four necessary conditions in the classic deadlock model.
questions.explanation: The classic conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. The presence of one condition alone does not prove a deadlock.

choices.text: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Circular wait
Guaranteed fairness

questions.prompt: In a paged virtual-memory system, what does a page table help translate?
questions.objective: Describe the role of page tables in virtual-to-physical address translation.
questions.explanation: A page table maps a process's virtual pages to physical memory frames, subject to access and presence information maintained by the operating system and hardware.

choices.text: Virtual pages to physical frames
DNS names to MAC addresses
Files to CPU time slices
Kernel calls to Ethernet ports

questions.prompt: Paging with fixed-size pages and frames eliminates external fragmentation, though some internal fragmentation can remain.
questions.objective: Compare external and internal fragmentation in paging.
questions.explanation: Fixed-size allocation avoids the external-fragmentation problem of requiring a contiguous free region of a particular size. The final page of an allocation may still be only partly used.

choices.text: True
False

questions.prompt: On a typical Linux file, what permissions does mode 644 represent?
questions.objective: Interpret a common numeric Linux permission mode.
questions.explanation: The owner has read and write (6); the group and others each have read (4). The digits are sums of read=4, write=2, and execute=1.

choices.text: Owner read/write; group read; others read
Everyone has read, write, and execute
Owner execute only; everyone else has no access
Group write only

questions.prompt: In a Linux shell, which command changes a file's permission mode: `chown` or `____`?
questions.objective: Choose the basic Linux command for changing permission bits.
questions.explanation: chmod changes permission bits. chown changes the owning user or group.

questions.prompt: What is a common purpose of a hardware interrupt?
questions.objective: Explain how devices can notify the processor that attention is needed.
questions.explanation: An interrupt lets a device signal an event that needs handling, rather than requiring the processor to continuously poll that device.

choices.text: Notify the processor that an event needs attention
Translate a hostname into an IP address
Allocate every process the same address space
Replace the operating-system kernel

questions.prompt: Which description best matches direct memory access (DMA)?
questions.objective: Describe how DMA can reduce CPU involvement in bulk data movement.
questions.explanation: A DMA-capable device or controller can move blocks of data between a device and memory with less per-byte CPU copying; the CPU still configures and coordinates the transfer.

choices.text: A controller transfers data between a device and memory with less CPU copying.
A program resolves an IP address to a MAC address.
The CPU is never involved in device I/O.
A disk stores every process in one shared file.

questions.prompt: In a typical UEFI-based startup, what is the bootloader's role after firmware initialization?
questions.objective: Place the bootloader in the firmware-to-operating-system startup sequence.
questions.explanation: Firmware initializes hardware and selects a boot target; a bootloader then loads or starts the operating-system kernel. Exact startup details vary by platform and configuration.

choices.text: Load or start the operating-system kernel
Assign a DHCP lease to every network device
Compile user applications during every boot
Format every mounted file system

questions.prompt: A Linux learner wants to show the current working directory in a terminal. Which command should they run?
questions.objective: Identify a basic Linux shell command from its effect.
questions.explanation: `pwd` prints the current working directory. It does not change directories; `cd` is used for that.

choices.text: pwd
chmod
mkdir
kill
